# A quaternion-lift argument for the Barnes–Wall orbifold anomaly

**26 November 2026 — Proposed proof; exact finite calculations reproduced internally; external expert review pending.** This text and the accompanying code were generated by coordinated AI agents. Separate agents performed the internal mathematical reviews and two different implementations of the lift calculation. No external expert has verified the argument, and no priority claim is made.

## Abstract and attribution

Keller, Ashley Winter Roberts and Jeremy Roberts constructed a holomorphic orbifold of the rank-128 Barnes–Wall lattice VOA conditional on the vanishing of an extraspecial-group anomaly [KRR, Conjecture 5.2]. We give a candidate argument for that vanishing. A compatible lift of a specific generalized quaternion group of order 16 removes the residual anomaly that cyclic tests alone cannot detect. We also give a direct proof that all involutions in the prescribed extraspecial action are standard lifts. A block argument proves the compatibility of the quaternion lift analytically. Exact finite calculations corroborate this argument and the source phase formulas; a separate implementation reconstructs them by a different method.

The Barnes–Wall action, proposed orbifold, twisted-module calculations and spectral analysis are due to KRR. The contribution proposed here is the compatible quaternion lift and its use with established group cohomology, together with the explicit standardness argument. The result does not concern the existence of an extremal VOA at central charge 48.

## 1. Statement and conventions

Let $L=BW(7)$, with exactly the ordered lattice basis of [KRR, (A.1.1)]. Let
$$
E=2^{1+14}_+
$$
act on $V_L$ through the sign lifts of [KRR, (2.2.1)–(2.2.4), Theorem 3.5]. Write $z=-I$ for its central involution, $A=E/\langle z\rangle\cong\mathbb F_2^{14}$, and $\pi:E\to A$. The quadratic form associated with this central extension is
$$
Q(s,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{7}s_it_i.
$$
Thus a lift of $a\in A$ has square $z^{Q(a)}$. We identify $H^3(G,U(1))$ with $H^4(G,\mathbb Z)$ for a finite group $G$.

**Proposed theorem.** The anomaly $\alpha\in H^3(E,U(1))$ of the specified action on $V_{BW(7)}$ is zero.

The theorem is about this particular action, including its lattice-VOA phases. Lattice isometries without their compatible lifts would not suffice.

All matrices below act on row lattice coordinates from the right. Products of lifts are read in the corresponding order. The quotient quadratic form $Q$, the conformal weight $\rho$, and the quadratic sign exponents $q_R$ are different objects.

## 2. A cohomological detection lemma

We use the extraspecial-group computation of [JFT, §3.3]. At width seven it gives
$$
H^4(E,\mathbb Z)\cong(\mathbb Z/2)^{454}\oplus\mathbb Z/4.
\tag{1}
$$
The image $X$ of inflation from $H^4(A,\mathbb Z)$ is elementary abelian of dimension 455, hence is exactly the 2-torsion subgroup. These dimensions follow directly from the filtration in that section: $H^4(A,\mathbb Z)$ has dimension $14+\binom{14}{2}+\binom{14}{3}=469$, and the inflation kernel has dimension 14. This uses the corrected rank obtained from the filtration, rather than the typographical rank formula noted in [KRR, §5.3].

### 2.1 The distinguished quadratic class

Let $x_i\in H^1(A,\mathbb F_2)$ be coordinates and $\beta$ the integral Bockstein. Put
$$
q=Q(\beta x_1,\ldots,\beta x_{14})\in H^4(A,\mathbb Z),
\qquad \widetilde q=\pi^*q.
$$
Here the variables in the quadratic polynomial are integral classes of degree two. Reduction modulo two sends $q$ to $Q(x)^2$. Since $Q$ is the extension class, $\pi^*Q=0$ in mod-2 cohomology. Consequently $\widetilde q$ has zero mod-2 reduction and is divisible by two in $H^4(E,\mathbb Z)$.

Choose a quaternion subgroup $H\cong Q_8$ whose image in $A$ is an anisotropic plane: its basis $a,b$ satisfies $Q(a)=Q(b)=1$ and $B_Q(a,b)=1$. The bilinear condition is essential. On that plane the extension form is
$$
Q_H(x,y)=x^2+xy+y^2.
$$
Write $X=\beta x$, $Y=\beta y$. The integral Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre differential used in [JFT, §3.3] is $d_3(\ell)=\beta(\ell Q_H)$. Its reductions give $d_3(x)=X^2$ and $d_3(y)=Y^2$. Thus the inflation image in total degree four is the nonzero one-dimensional quotient spanned by $XY$; no later differential enters bidegree $(4,0)$. Therefore
$$
\widetilde q|_H=\operatorname{Inf}(X^2+XY+Y^2)
              =\operatorname{Inf}(XY)\ne0.
\tag{2}
$$
In particular $\widetilde q$ is the unique nonzero element divisible by two in (1). This supplies the quaternion-detection fact directly, without relying on wording that omits the anisotropic-plane condition.

### 2.2 Cyclic restrictions and Boolean cubics

Put $U_i=\beta x_i$. An explicit integral basis for $H^4(A,\mathbb Z)$, compatible with [JFT, §3.1], is
$$
U_i^2,\qquad U_iU_j\ (i<j),\qquad
\beta(x_ix_jx_k)\ (i<j<k).
$$
On the line generated by $a$, these restrict respectively to $a_i$, $a_ia_j$, and $a_ia_ja_k$, times the generator of $H^4(C_2,\mathbb Z)$. For the third family, if $t$ generates $H^1(C_2,\mathbb F_2)$, then $\beta(t^3)$ generates $H^4(C_2,\mathbb Z)$. The resulting degree-one, degree-two and degree-three squarefree monomials are linearly independent as Boolean functions, and their number is 469. This gives an identification with squarefree Boolean polynomials of degree at most three and zero constant term, under which cyclic restriction is evaluation. The explicit type-I, type-II and type-III cocycles in [Yu, (6)] give the same description.

We need the following elementary lemma, stated only at the dimension needed here.

**Boolean lemma.** If a squarefree polynomial $f(u,v)$ of degree at most three on $\mathbb F_2^7\oplus\mathbb F_2^7$ vanishes on every point with $\sum u_iv_i=0$, then
$$
f=Q\left(\delta+\sum_i\beta_i u_i+\sum_i\gamma_i v_i\right)
\tag{3}
$$
in the Boolean ring, where each coordinate satisfies $x^2=x$.

**Proof.** The restrictions $f(u,0)$ and $f(0,v)$ vanish, so uniqueness of squarefree polynomial representation removes all terms using just one block of variables. Evaluating $u=e_i$ with arbitrary $v_i=0$, and then $v=e_i$ with arbitrary $u_i=0$, leaves only
$$
f=\sum_i u_iv_i\left(A_i+\sum_{j\ne i}B_{ij}u_j+\sum_{j\ne i}C_{ij}v_j\right).
$$
Set $u_i=v_i=u_k=v_k=1$ for distinct $i,k$, all other coordinates initially zero. The point is singular. Varying $u_j$ for $j\notin\{i,k\}$ gives $B_{ij}=B_{kj}$. Thus every off-diagonal column is constant, $B_{ij}=\beta_j$. Likewise $C_{ij}=\gamma_j$. At the original two-pair point,
$$
A_i+\beta_i+\gamma_i=A_k+\beta_k+\gamma_k.
$$
Call the common value $\delta$. Expanding (3) with $x^2=x$ gives the displayed expression. $\square$

The inflation-kernel differential in [JFT, §3.3] is $\ell\mapsto Sq^1(\ell Q)$. Under the preceding restriction description, these classes are the Boolean polynomials $\ell Q$: the integral Bockstein of the homogeneous cubic $\ell Q$ reduces to $Sq^1(\ell Q)$, and its cyclic restriction is $\ell(a)Q(a)$.

**Detection lemma.** A class $\eta\in H^4(E,\mathbb Z)$ is zero if it restricts to zero on every cyclic involution subgroup and on one quaternion subgroup with anisotropic quotient plane.

**Proof.** If $\eta$ had order four, then $2\eta=\widetilde q$, contradicting (2) and $\eta|_H=0$. Hence $\eta$ is 2-torsion and lies in the inflation image $X$. Write $\eta=\pi^*\nu$. Each nonzero singular vector of $A$ has an order-two lift, on which $\pi$ is an isomorphism. Therefore the Boolean polynomial for $\nu$ vanishes on $Q=0$. Equation (3) and the inflation-kernel description leave only $\eta=\delta\widetilde q$. Equation (2) then forces $\delta=0$. $\square$

## 3. Standardness of the prescribed involutions

This section proves the necessary cyclic condition directly. It does not use the assertion that every tensor word containing a $Y=XZ$ factor is fixed-point-free: for example, $Y_1Y_2$ is an involution with a 64-dimensional real fixed space. The proof below also covers these even-$Y$ tensor words.

Label the KRR lattice basis by subsets $I$ of seven tensor factors. Modulo two, its parity-zero space $V_0$ consists of odd-cardinality subsets and $V_1$ of even-cardinality subsets. From [KRR, (A.2.8)–(A.2.11)],
$$
X_i=I+A_i^+,\qquad Z_i=I+A_i^-,
$$
where $A_i^+$ adds factor $i$ to an odd subset when absent, $A_i^-$ removes it when present, and both kill $V_1$. Every product $A_i^\epsilon A_j^\eta$ is zero. Hence
$$
R=z^\epsilon\prod_iX_i^{s_i}Z_i^{t_i}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
R-I=N=\sum_i(s_iA_i^++t_iA_i^-)
\tag{4}
$$
over $\mathbb F_2$.

Put $W=\operatorname{span}(e_2,\ldots,e_7)$ and split
$$
V_0=\Lambda^{\rm odd}W\oplus e_1\wedge\Lambda^{\rm even}W.
$$
Write the $V_0$ component of a vector as $(x,y)$. On either parity subspace define the complementary-pair quadratic
$$
\mathfrak q(u)=\sum_{\{I,I^c\}}u_Iu_{I^c},
\tag{5}
$$
with each unordered complementary pair of subsets of the six factors counted once. Complementation preserves parity.

For the canonical sign lifts in KRR the phase exponents are
$$
q_{X_1}=\mathfrak q_{\rm odd}(x),\qquad
q_{Z_1}=\mathfrak q_{\rm even}(y),\qquad
q_{X_i}=q_{Z_i}=0\quad(i\ge2).
\tag{6}
$$
To see this directly, decompose the binary half-Gram matrix as $H=H_1+H_2$ using [KRR, Lemmas A.1–A.3]. The matrix $H_2$ is supported on $V_0\times V_0$, while $H_1(e_I)=e_{I^c}$ when $1\in I$ and is zero otherwise. Since $A$ maps $V_0$ to $V_1$ and kills $V_1$, $H_2$ contributes nothing to the defect
$$
H-(I+A)H(I+A)^T=AH+HA^T+AHA^T.
$$
For $A_1^+$, the surviving term $AH_1$ pairs first-factor-absent odd subsets with their complementary six-factor subsets. For $A_1^-$, the term $H_1A^T$ gives the corresponding first-factor-present pairs. Taking the strict lower triangle gives (6); for the other factors the defect terms cancel as in KRR Lemmas A.3–A.4. Each first-factor quadratic has exactly 16 monomials. Both checkers also verify (6) coefficient by coefficient from the full half-Gram matrix.

These phases depend only on $V_0$, whose coordinates are unchanged by every binary generator. Thus the prescribed product lift has phase
$$
q_R=s_1\mathfrak q_{\rm odd}(x)+t_1\mathfrak q_{\rm even}(y).
\tag{7}
$$

Let
$$
C=\sum_{i=2}^7(s_i e_i\wedge+t_i\iota_i),\qquad
Q_0=\sum_{i=2}^7s_it_i.
$$
The Clifford relations in characteristic two give $C^2=Q_0I$. The polar form of (5) is
$$
B(u,v)=[e_2\wedge\cdots\wedge e_7](u\wedge v).
$$
Wedge and contraction are self-adjoint for this pairing, so
$$
B(Cu,Cv)=Q_0B(u,v).
$$
The function $\mathfrak q(Cu)+Q_0\mathfrak q(u)$ is therefore linear. It vanishes on each coordinate vector $e_I$: the support of $Ce_I$ consists of subsets differing from $I$ in one bit, whereas complementary subsets differ in six bits. Hence
$$
\mathfrak q(Cu)=Q_0\mathfrak q(u).
\tag{8}
$$

For a binary fixed vector, (4) gives
$$
Cx+t_1y=0,\qquad s_1x+Cy=0.
\tag{9}
$$
An involution has $Q_0=s_1t_1$. If $(s_1,t_1)=(0,0)$, (7) is zero. If $(1,0)$, then $x=Cy$, and (8) gives $\mathfrak q(x)=0$. The case $(0,1)$ is analogous. If $(1,1)$, then $y=Cx$ and $\mathfrak q(y)=\mathfrak q(x)$, again making (7) zero.

The phase therefore vanishes on the entire binary fixed space. Every integral fixed vector reduces to that space, so all the prescribed involution lifts are standard. The central involution already has trivial phase.

The real eigenvalue multiplicities from [KRR, (3.2.2)–(3.2.5)] then give twisted ground-state weight 4 for a noncentral involution and 8 for the central involution. Their cyclic types $2^2\rho\bmod2$ are zero. This proves all involution restrictions required by the detection lemma.

For the orbifold consequence below, also note that every order-four element of $E$ squares to $-I$, so its lattice isometry is fixed-point-free and its prescribed lift is standard. Its twisted ground-state weight is 6 by [KRR, §3.2]. Thus every nontrivial $E$-twisted sector has ground weight at least four.

The optional finite confirmation enumerates all 8,256 singular quotient vectors: 2,080 have identically zero phase, and all 6,176 remaining phase forms vanish on the complete binary kernel. It checks 197,632 kernel-basis values and 3,063,296 polarization values, without integral-nullspace or floating-point assumptions.

## 4. The compatible quaternion lift

In Cartesian tensor coordinates put
$$
X=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad Y=XZ.
$$
Tensor positions are numbered $1,\ldots,7$ in KRR order: position $a$ is source bit $i[7-a]$. Define
$$
a=Y_1,\qquad b=Z_1Y_2,\qquad
g=\frac{(I+Y_1)(X_3+Z_3)}2.
\tag{10}
$$
The factors in $g$ commute. Since $Y_1^T=-Y_1$, $Y_1^2=-I$ and $(X_3+Z_3)^2=2I$, the matrix $g$ is orthogonal. Direct tensor multiplication gives
$$
g^2=a,\qquad a^2=b^2=g^4=z=-I,\qquad bgbg=z.
\tag{11}
$$
For the last relation, conjugation by $b$ negates $Y_1$ and fixes $X_3+Z_3$, giving $bgb^{-1}=g^{-1}$.

### 4.1 Integral rows and the lattice subgroup

Write $e_i$ for the ordered KRR lattice basis vector with seven-bit index $i$. Put $p_i=(7-|i|)\bmod2$, where $|i|$ counts one-bits, and let $i^S$ denote toggling the positions in $S$. The source rows [KRR, (A.2.5)–(A.2.6)] imply
$$
e_i(X_3+Z_3)=2^{p_i}e_{i^{\{3\}}},\qquad
e_iY_1=(-1)^{i_1}\bigl(e_i-2^{p_i}e_{i^{\{1\}}}\bigr).
$$
Toggling one bit exchanges $p_i$ and $1-p_i$. Substitution into (10) therefore gives
$$
e_ig=
\begin{cases}
2^{p_i}e_{i^{\{3\}}}-e_{i^{\{1,3\}}},&i_1=0,\\
e_{i^{\{1,3\}}},&i_1=1.
\end{cases}
$$
Thus $g$ has integral lattice coordinates. Equation (11) gives $g^8=I$, so its inverse is integral as well; hence $g\in\operatorname{Aut}(L)$.

The matrix $g$ has order eight, and $b$ is not a power of $g$: it conjugates $g$ to $g^{-1}\ne g$. The relations consequently give $\langle g,b\rangle\cong Q_{16}$ of order sixteen, with $\langle a,b\rangle\cong Q_8$. The images of $a,b$ in $A$ satisfy $Q(a)=Q(b)=B_Q(a,b)=1$, so their plane is the required anisotropic plane.

### 4.2 A block lemma for canonical lifts

Let $G$ be the KRR Gram matrix and $H$ its lower half: the strictly lower entries are those of $G$, the diagonal is $G_{ii}/2$, and the upper entries are zero. The lattice cocycle is $\epsilon(v,w)=(-1)^{vHw^T}$. For a lattice isometry $R$, the canonical lift is
$$
B_R=\operatorname{strictlower}(H-RHR^T)\bmod2,
\qquad
\widehat R(e^v)=(-1)^{vB_Rv^T}e^{vR}.
\tag{12}
$$
The defect is symmetric modulo two with zero diagonal, and $B_R+B_R^T$ equals it; hence (12) is a valid cocycle lift. Its phase is zero on every lattice basis vector. We continue to read lift products in right-action order, consistently with row coordinates.

**Block lemma.** Suppose the lattice basis is partitioned into blocks on each of which $H$ restricts to zero modulo two. On the subgroup of lattice isometries preserving the span of each block, canonical lifts form a group homomorphism.

**Proof.** For such an isometry $R$, the rows indexed by one block are supported in that block. Thus both $H$ and $RHR^T$ vanish on the block modulo two, as does $B_R$. The phase $q_R(v)=vB_Rv^T$ consequently vanishes for every vector supported in a single block. For two such isometries $R,S$, the product lift has phase
$$
q_R(e_i)+q_S(e_iR)=0
$$
on every basis vector, just as the canonical lift of $RS$ does. Two lifts of the same lattice isometry differ on the lattice group algebra by a lattice character, as follows by dividing their cocycle-lift identities. A character trivial on the basis is trivial everywhere. Their Heisenberg actions also agree, proving equality of the VOA automorphisms. $\square$

To apply the lemma, let $d(i,j)$ be Hamming distance. The KRR basis (A.1.1) gives the exact Gram formula
$$
G_{ij}
=2^{\lceil(7-|i|)/2\rceil+\lceil(7-|j|)/2\rceil+|i\cap j|-4}
=2^{\,3-d(i,j)/2+(p_i+p_j)/2}.
$$
The exponent is integral, and $H_{ii}=2^{2+p_i}$ is even. Partition the basis according to its four bits in positions $4,5,6,7$. This gives sixteen blocks of eight vectors. Within a block, $d(i,j)\le3$, so the Gram exponent is at least two. Every within-block Gram entry is therefore divisible by four, and $H$ restricts to zero modulo two. No condition on pairings between distinct blocks is required.

The matrices $X_1,Z_1,X_2,Z_2$ preserve each block by their source row formulas. The row formula in §4.1 shows that $g$ does too. The block lemma thus applies to all matrices needed here.

### 4.3 Agreement with the prescribed action

Retain the prescribed products
$\widehat a=\widehat X_1\widehat Z_1$ and
$\widehat b=\widehat Z_1\widehat X_2\widehat Z_2$.
Their generator lifts are exactly the canonical lifts of KRR. The block lemma makes them the canonical lifts of $a,b$ and lifts every relation (11). In particular,
$$
\widehat g^{\,2}=\widehat a,\qquad
\widehat a^{\,2}=\widehat b^{\,2}=\widehat z,\qquad
\widehat b\widehat g\widehat b\widehat g=\widehat z.
\tag{13}
$$
No character correction is required. Since the canonical lift homomorphism projects to the original lattice action, it embeds this $Q_{16}$, gives $\widehat g$ actual order eight, and agrees with the prescribed $E$ action on the common $Q_8$.

The two accompanying exact implementations independently reproduce the lattice and phase identities as supplementary verification of this analytic argument. The argument itself requires no enumeration of 128-dimensional phase coefficients. It makes no assertion about lifting the whole Barnes–Wall normalizer.

## 5. Restriction through $Q_{16}$

The eigenvalues of $g$ are the primitive eighth roots with exponents $1,3,5,7$, each of multiplicity 32. The matrix is fixed-point-free, and (13) gives actual lift order eight. Its standard twisted ground-state weight is
$$
\rho_g=\frac{32}{4\cdot8^2}(7+15+15+7)=\frac{11}{2}.
$$
The cyclic type is $8^2\rho_g=352\equiv0\pmod8$. Therefore the anomaly of the $Q_{16}$ action restricts to zero on its $C_8$ subgroup.

For completeness, the needed quaternion-group restriction statement follows from the free $S^3$ action. A finite subgroup $\Gamma\subset SU(2)$ acts freely on $S^3$; the Gysin sequence for the associated sphere bundle identifies
$$
H^4(B\Gamma,\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/|\Gamma|
$$
with generator the second Chern class of the defining two-dimensional representation. Restriction to a subgroup sends that generator to the corresponding generator and is surjective. This is also the fact recorded in [Yu, (14)].

In particular, restriction from $H^4(Q_{16},\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z/16$ to either $C_8$ or $Q_8$ is a surjection onto $\mathbb Z/8$. Both have the same kernel, the unique order-two subgroup. Vanishing on $C_8$ therefore implies vanishing on $Q_8$.

The use of a quaternion subgroup inside a binary dihedral group to eliminate an extraspecial-group cohomology class also appears in [JFT, printed p. 30]. The additional point here is the compatible lift (13) for the prescribed Barnes–Wall VOA action.

Anomaly restriction is natural and the actions agree on $Q_8$, so $\alpha|_{Q_8}=0$. Section 3 gives all cyclic involution restrictions zero. The detection lemma now gives $\alpha=0$, proving the proposed theorem. $\square$

## 6. Intended orbifold consequence and its scope

The theorem removes the anomaly hypothesis in [KRR, Conjecture 5.2]. The intended extension is the **full $E$-orbifold**, namely the sum, over conjugacy classes, of the trivial-centralizer modules after choosing an anomaly trivialization. It is not a statement that some holomorphic extension of $V_L^E$ exists if and only if the anomaly vanishes: the parent $V_L$ is always a holomorphic extension of its fixed-point algebra.

Here is the extension step explicitly. Put $W=V_L^E$. The positive definite unimodular lattice VOA $V_L$ is strongly rational and holomorphic. The finite 2-group $E$ is solvable, so [CM, Corollary 5.25] gives the regularity needed for $W$ to be strongly rational. By [GR, Theorem 3.1],
$$
\operatorname{Rep}(W)\simeq Z(\mathrm{Vec}_E^{\alpha}).
$$
All nonvacuum simple $W$-modules have positive conformal weight: the untwisted constituents occur in positive weights of $V_L$, and the nontrivial twisted sectors have ground weight at least four by the preceding standardness calculation and [KRR, §3.2]. Thus the positive ribbon structure is the one induced by the VOA, as in [GR, §§2.1–2.2]; we may transport the trivial-twist algebra below through this equivalence.

After trivializing $\alpha$, take the group algebra $\mathbb C[E]$ in $Z(\mathrm{Vec}_E)$, graded by group elements and acted on by conjugation. It is a connected, separable, braided-commutative algebra with trivial twist. Its dimension is $|E|$, so its local-module category has dimension one. Its decomposition into simple objects is
$$
\mathbb C[E]=\bigoplus_{[g]}[g,\mathbf 1_{C_E(g)}].
$$
The extension correspondence [HKL, Theorems 3.2, 3.4–3.6; GR, §2.2] therefore gives a strongly rational holomorphic VOA extension of $W$. Equivalently, it is the $K=E$, trivial-discrete-torsion case of [EG, Corollary 2 and (3.5)]. It shares the conformal vector and central charge 128. This identifies the particular full-group orbifold, rather than the parent-VOA extension corresponding to $K=1$.

The no-low-weight-state analysis in [KRR, (5.3.3)] now applies: below weight four, the extension contains only the vacuum and its Virasoro descendants. To see that the primary gap is exactly four without assuming a unitary extension, let $F_r$ be the $E$-invariant Heisenberg space of weight $r$. KRR §6.2 gives $\dim F_2=\dim F_3=1$ and $\dim F_4=2797$. The last count also follows directly from the defining representation $U=\mathbb C^{128}$:
$$
\dim(\operatorname{Sym}^4 U)^E
 =\frac{2\binom{131}{4}+(32768-2)\binom{65}{2}}{32768}=2795,
$$
with one further invariant from each of $U\otimes U$ and $\operatorname{Sym}^2 U$ in the weight-four Heisenberg decomposition. Since $L_1:F_4\to F_3$ and $L_2:F_4\to F_2$, their common kernel has dimension at least 2795. The positive Virasoro algebra is generated by $L_1,L_2$, so every vector in that kernel is primary. The full orbifold therefore has primary gap four. No claim about VOA unitarity or uniqueness is made.
